questions.q: What Kubernetes kind does Argo Rollouts use in place of a standard Deployment to enable native canary traffic shifting?
options: StatefulSet
Rollout
Job
HorizontalPodAutoscaler
questions.explain: A Rollout keeps the same container spec as a Deployment but adds a strategy block -- setWeight and pause steps -- that a plain Deployment doesn't understand.

questions.q: In the AnalysisTemplate, what does successCondition: result[0] < 0.01 actually gate?
options: Whether the container image was built successfully
Whether the catalog entry resolves correctly
Whether the canary's error rate stays under 1%, as measured by the Prometheus query
Whether the GitOps repo has any uncommitted changes
questions.explain: The query divides 5xx request rate by total request rate for the canary revision; the rollout step only proceeds if that ratio stays under 1%.

questions.q: Why does the rollout set analysis.startingStep: 2 instead of running the analysis from the very first step?
options: So the analysis only starts once traffic first reaches real users at a later step, not during the very first weight that's still settling
Because AnalysisTemplates are not allowed to run during step 1 by Argo Rollouts' design
To save on Prometheus query costs regardless of correctness
Because step 1 always fails the error-rate check by default
questions.explain: startingStep: 2 means every pause from that point on is backed by a real automated check, rather than running analysis during the earliest, still-settling traffic shift.

questions.q: When the canary's error rate crosses the failureLimit threshold, what happens without any human running a command?
options: Nothing happens until someone manually reviews the dashboard
The entire Application is deleted from ArgoCD
ArgoCD automatically reverts the Git commit that introduced the change
Argo Rollouts aborts the rollout on its own, scales the canary to zero, and returns all traffic to the stable revision
questions.explain: Automated rollback means Argo Rollouts itself aborts the canary and restores traffic to the stable revision -- no manual kubectl rollback or incident call required.

questions.q: After an automated rollback, why does the Application in ArgoCD still show the commit that introduced the bad release as OutOfSync, rather than disappearing without a trace?
options: Because this setup is still GitOps end to end -- the failure and the rollback state are both visible through the same Git and ArgoCD reconciliation Chapter 4 already established
Because ArgoCD automatically deletes the Application on any failure
Because OutOfSync always means the cluster has no record of the deployment
Because Argo Rollouts bypasses ArgoCD entirely during a rollback
questions.explain: The Rollout and AnalysisTemplate are just more YAML in the overlay ArgoCD syncs, so the whole canary and its rollback stay visible through ordinary GitOps reconciliation rather than vanishing.
